entries.consequence: Who may add a standing rule to your ledger. Ledger page only: you add rules by hand on the Ledger page, and a /Request typed in a chat is refused with a note pointing you there. Ledger page and /Request: you add rules on the Ledger page or by typing /Request, /RequestSession, /RequestTree or /RequestThread in a chat. Agents too: as well as both of those, your agents may turn something you said into a rule, filed under the agent's name; the two settings nested below decide whether an unsure agent asks first and whether an agent's rule waits for your approval. In the first two choices agents neither file rules nor ask you whether to; they carry on with the work. The reset buttons on the Ledger page are yours in every choice.
capabilities: One choice decides every door into the rules ledger: the page, the chat command, and your agents.
risks: Agents too: an offhand remark can become a rule that steers later sessions until you find it on the Ledger page and remove it.
Ledger page only: a rule typed as /Request in a chat is refused, so a habit of typing rules in chat stops working until you change this.

entries.consequence: The older on/off form of "Who adds standing rules": it reads on when that choice is Agents too and off otherwise, and choosing there is what changes it. Your agents can notice when you say something meant to last — "always ask before spending money", "from now on keep it short" — and write it down as a standing rule in your own words. Off: only you file rules, by typing /Request. On: the agent decides when something you said is a rule and files it, marked as filed by that agent; the chat shows you a line saying what was filed and where, and every later session reads it until you edit or delete the entry by hand. When an agent is unsure it suggests the rule instead and you accept or decline it. This covers the standing-rule ledgers only — your agents' durable notes, research findings, tasks and messages have their own tools and are not changed here. At the Guided level agents only read, so nothing is filed either way.
capabilities: You say a thing once, in your own words, and it keeps applying — no command to remember.
risks: On, an offhand remark can become a rule that steers every later session until you find it in the rules panel and delete it by hand.
An agent can only name the scope keys it was shown, but a mistaken key puts a rule on the wrong circle until you see it there.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js

entries.consequence: When your agent is not sure you meant a standing rule, or not sure who it covers, it files nothing and ends its reply with one short question; your yes files your original sentence. Off: the agent uses the narrowest reading and says so.
capabilities: A doubtful remark never becomes a rule behind your back: the agent asks once, briefly, and waits for your yes.
risks: On, you will be asked a short question now and then, and a rule you did mean waits on file until you answer it.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/r-ledger-agent-gate.js

entries.consequence: This is what you chose when you set the program up: whether the assistant works inside one folder, inside the projects you add, or anywhere on this computer. You can narrow it here at any time. Widening it asks you the same question the setup did.
entries.readOnlyReason: Read-only here because ordinary settings must never be able to widen the installation boundary. The displayed level comes from machine.json, where first-run setup records it. To change it, run ToolsEnabled setup again yourself; existing sessions keep their current ceiling and new sessions use the newly recorded level.
capabilities: A wider level lets an assistant read and change more of this computer, so it can finish tasks that reach outside one folder.
risks: Everything outside the level is refused today; widening it removes that refusal for every assistant at once, not only the one you had in mind.

At the wider levels an assistant can run a project's own setup, build and test scripts. Those are written by whoever wrote the project and its dependencies, not by this product, and they can do anything your account can do.

externalStep.whatItDoes: Lets you run a project's own setup yourself, on the rare occasion that the project asks Windows for administrator rights while it installs or builds.
capabilitiesGained: A project whose setup genuinely needs an administrator can finish, so its build and tests can run here like any other project's.
risks: A project's setup scripts are written by other people. Running one as an administrator gives that code full rights on this computer for as long as it runs, and this product cannot tell you in advance what it will do with them.
This is the one place where the thing asking for administrator rights is not this product and not Windows, but a project you pointed it at.
externalStep.frequencyBecause: Node projects install into their own folder and their build and test scripts run with whatever rights they were started with, so the overwhelming majority never ask for anything. The exceptions are packages that register a Windows service, install a driver, or write somewhere machine-wide from an install script. Derived from where npm and its lifecycle scripts write by default, not from whether a prompt appeared on any particular computer.

steps.do: Read what the project's setup actually runs before you decide. Its package.json lists any preinstall, install and postinstall scripts, and those are the ones that run without being asked for.
steps.why: This is the step this product cannot do for you in the useful sense: it can run the scripts, but it cannot judge them. You can.

steps.do: If you accept it, open Windows PowerShell as an administrator, change to the project folder, and run the install command yourself once.
steps.why: This product does not ask Windows for administrator rights, does not pass them on to a project's scripts, and does not change any Windows security setting to get around the prompt. Doing this step yourself is what keeps that true.

steps.do: Come back and run it here as normal.
steps.why: The part that needed an administrator is already done, so the ordinary run finishes without it.

externalStep.verify: The step that stopped now completes, and this product stops reporting that something it ran asked for administrator rights.
externalStep.withoutIt: The setting stays on and saves, and everything else at your level keeps working. A project whose setup asks for administrator rights stops at that step and says so plainly — including when Windows refuses the request on its own because there was nowhere to show you the approval box, which it misleadingly reports as you having cancelled it. Nothing is retried with more rights, nothing is recorded as done, and no partial result is thrown away.

entries.consequence: On, every agent this program starts is handed a few short lines at the start of its session saying which tools this computer actually offers at your permission level, which ones it reaches for constantly, and which ones this level withholds -- so you never have to teach an agent what exists or explain why a withheld tool is not a breakage. The note is generated from the real permitted list at the moment the session starts, so it cannot claim a tool your level refuses. Off, agents are told nothing about the toolkit and only discover tools you name yourself.
capabilities: A new agent knows which Fleet tools it can reach at the current permission level.
risks: The note rides at the start of each session, so the model provider receives a short description of which tool families this computer offers, and it costs a few hundred tokens per session.

entries.consequence: Choose which tools new agent sessions receive. Only uses ToolsEnabled API tools and restricts native tools. Optimized works with Claude only: it adds Claude’s file search, skills, planning and tool search to the API tools. Sessions on other providers do not start while Optimized is selected. Enabled, the default, offers both the API and the provider’s native tools. Disabled withholds the ToolsEnabled API and keeps native tools within the existing role and permission limits. Existing sessions keep their captured choice. API outcome summaries follow Tool activity audit; native tool activity is not added to that API audit.
capabilities: Choose API tools only, API tools with a few Claude native tools, both full tool sets, or native tools for new sessions.
API calls keep their permissions, approvals and required signed security records. Tool activity audit controls outcome summaries.
risks: Only can prevent a task when the API has no working equivalent for a native tool.

Optimized works with Claude only. Codex, Gemini, Grok and local sessions do not start while it is selected. Claude’s selected native actions follow its permissions and are not in the ToolsEnabled API audit.
Enabled lets an agent choose native tools whose actions are not in the ToolsEnabled API audit.
Disabled removes API-based coordination and integrations. Providers with no native tools may have no tools available.

entries.consequence: Let agents change ToolsEnabled's own source inside a checkout through the ToolsEnabled file tools. Off keeps the integrity fence: host.write_file and host.patch_file refuse the product code folders (src, shell, bin, tools, scripts, sidecars, packages, captures, scratch, tmp) inside every ToolsEnabled checkout, which with Available tool sets on Only stops an agent from developing the product at all. On lifts that one rule for checkouts that are not the running installation. The running installation, state, config, KILLSWITCH, .git, node_modules, the package manifests and the policy documents stay refused. Read on every call.
capabilities: Agents can develop ToolsEnabled itself inside a checkout you made for them, without leaving the audited ToolsEnabled tools.
risks: While it is on, a confused or hijacked agent can rewrite product code in any ToolsEnabled checkout under your profile; only the running installation and its integrity anchors stay protected.

entries.consequence: When one of your assistants starts another one, this decides where the new one appears. Left as it is, a new assistant joins your tree when the one that started it is already on your tree, and runs on its own otherwise. Set to always on your tree, every assistant an assistant starts is drawn as a circle under it, with its own name, its own conversation and the same stop button as one you started by hand; a start is refused, and says so, when the assistant asking is not itself on a tree. Set to never on your tree, they run on their own the way they always have: bounded, recorded and reachable through the request ledger, but nothing is drawn for you to see. This is a separate question from whether your assistants use this program’s tools at all, which the row above decides.
capabilities: An assistant that another assistant started shows up as a circle you can read, talk to and stop, instead of working somewhere you cannot see.
You settle it once for every assistant on this computer, rather than hoping each one makes the same choice about where to hand work down.
risks: Drawing them on your tree makes each one a live conversation on this computer, and this computer holds only so many of those at once; past that a start is refused by name.
Always on your tree refuses a start whenever the assistant asking is not itself on a tree, so an assistant working on its own will be told no rather than quietly starting a helper.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-subagent-route.js subagentRoute() returns the one route a spawn may take and src/lib/tool-registry.js spawnSubagent obeys it, refusing by name rather than falling back to the other route. It never reads the Agent API row: that one decides whether an assistant also keeps its own built-in tool for this, which is a different question. A value nobody chose cannot force a route, so only user or installer provenance is read as a choice and anything unreadable leaves the shipped answer standing.

entries.consequence: On, every time you type something to an agent, it is handed up to three ToolsEnabled tools that might fit what you just said -- by exact id, with one line each -- so you do not have to know the name of the tool to get it used. Most of the time it is handed nothing at all: "hi", "thanks" and "keep going" get silence, and so does anything the match is not confident about. It only ever names tools your permission level actually offers. Off, agents are told nothing per message and find tools only from the session-start note above or from what you name yourself. The cost when it does speak is about a hundred and twenty tokens on that one message; your words are used to pick the tools and are not written down anywhere by this.
capabilities: You can ask for what you want in your own words -- "what is on my calendar today", "put this on my clipboard" -- and the agent is shown the tool that does it, instead of you having to know its id.
risks: When it does have something to say, the short list rides on that message, so the model provider receives up to three tool ids and their one-line descriptions along with what you typed.
A suggestion is only a suggestion: the agent may take the named tool when a different one, or none, was the better answer.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/capability-recall/index.js

entries.consequence: Full selects signed success and failure summaries for completed API tool calls. Essential keeps failure summaries and omits successful-call summaries. Off omits both kinds of tool summary. This preference is dormant unless activity auditing is explicitly enabled. Operational custody and permission checks remain active. Permissions, sandboxing, vault protection and approval enforcement do not change. Applies to the next completed call; existing history is kept. Native tools outside the API are outside this activity audit.

Essential saves successful-call recording work while keeping failure summaries.
Off removes tool-summary recording work and retains less activity history.
risks: Essential leaves no general summary of successful calls; Off also loses failure summaries and the usage measurements derived from those records.

Omitted summaries cannot be recovered later. Summary recording uses the existing best-effort recorder: write failures are reported and can leave gaps, even in Full. Explicitly enabled operation audit still takes time. Neither lighter choice guarantees a particular call speed.

entries.consequence: Fast, the default: when several assistants call tools at once, their calls run side by side. Calls that only read run together; calls that change something keep their order for each assistant, so an assistant's second change never overtakes its first. Records selected by Tool activity audit, and all required security records, are saved before the call answers. Records from calls that arrive together are saved in one batch instead of one at a time, and that saving happens on a helper thread instead of the thread that draws this window. Strict: the older behaviour, one call at a time per assistant and one record saved per call, which is slower and can make this window hesitate while many assistants are working. It applies to the next call; no restart is needed.
capabilities: Many assistants can work at once without waiting on each other or slowing the window down.
risks: Two assistants changing the same thing at the same time are ordered by the store they change, not by arrival at this computer, which is what already happens across two computers.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/throughput-mode.js reads the row; src/lib/tool-registry.js routes activity records through src/lib/audit-admission.js; src/mcp-server.js selects the dispatch scheduler for incoming calls.

entries.consequence: This exact model name is sent to your chosen provider. If the provider does not recognize it or rejects the request, the assistant tells you that the request failed; it does not silently switch to another model.
capabilities: Sends your chosen model name to the provider, so you get the model you meant.
risks: Very little. If the provider does not recognise the name it says the request failed; it is never quietly answered by a different model.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/providers/customer-model.js

entries.consequence: New interactive local agents and local workers use this exact installed model. A model selected for an individual agent wins. Until this default is set, the existing model name is retained for Ollama. An unavailable choice stops with its name; it is never replaced silently.
capabilities: Choose a fast local coordinator independently of the model used by tool requests.
risks: Larger models need more GPU memory and may take longer to load.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/agent-engine/local-node-process.js; src/lib/providers/local-node-runtime.js

entries.consequence: The model request tool uses this exact model on your configured provider. Until this default is set, it uses the existing model name above. Changing it does not change an interactive local agent's model.
capabilities: Choose the model used by tool requests separately from local agents.
risks: The selected model may use more memory or incur charges on a remote provider.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/providers/customer-model.js

entries.consequence: Require GPU requests all model layers on the GPU and verifies Ollama's memory report before sending your prompt and after generation. If the model does not fit, the request stops. Allow CPU fallback explicitly permits Ollama to split work with the CPU. CPU only requests zero GPU layers.
capabilities: Keep local agents and tool requests on the GPU, or explicitly choose CPU use.
risks: Requiring the GPU can refuse a model that would fit partly in system memory. CPU fallback can substantially slow replies.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/ollama-gpu.js; src/lib/agent-engine/local-node-process.js; src/lib/providers/customer-model.js; src/lib/providers/local-node-runtime.js

entries.consequence: Ollama receives this context size for every local request. Choose a whole number from 512 through 131072. Increasing it lets the model consider more history and tool descriptions, and also reserves more memory.
capabilities: Balance local conversation context against GPU memory use.
risks: A context that is too large can prevent full GPU residency. A small context may omit older conversation details inside Ollama.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/settings.js; src/lib/agent-engine/local-node-adapter.js; src/lib/providers/customer-model.js; src/lib/providers/local-node-runtime.js

entries.consequence: Fast asks Ollama to disable thinking so a short reply can begin promptly. Reasoning explicitly enables thinking; it shares the output budget with the answer. Model default omits the thinking option. A model that rejects the chosen mode reports that rejection.
capabilities: Choose quick coordination replies or additional reasoning on supported local models.
risks: Fast mode can reduce answer quality on difficult tasks. Reasoning can spend the output budget before producing an answer.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/agent-engine/local-node-adapter.js; src/lib/providers/customer-model.js; src/lib/providers/local-node-runtime.js

entries.consequence: Ask Ollama to keep the chosen model loaded for this many minutes after each local request, from 1 through 60. A following request can reuse the loaded weights; Ollama may still unload them to serve another model.
capabilities: Reduce repeated model loading between local coordination turns.
risks: The loaded model continues to occupy GPU or system memory while idle.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/local-model-options.js; src/lib/settings.js; src/lib/agent-engine/local-node-adapter.js; src/lib/providers/customer-model.js; src/lib/providers/local-node-runtime.js

entries.consequence: When the allowance on the account an assistant is using runs out, the assistant stops and tells you which account is spent and which of your other accounts with the same service is ready, so you choose. It never moves the work onto another of your accounts with the same service by itself.
capabilities: Keeps every move between your own accounts with one service in your hands: nothing is spent on another of those accounts until you choose it.
risks: Work that reaches an account's limit waits until you switch accounts, choose a different service, or the allowance resets.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/multi-account/rotation.js resolveAccountForSession stops every start whose account cannot serve, names the account that is ready, and never selects another account of the same program by itself, whatever a caller, the account registry or this row carries; src/lib/settings.js reads a stored retired `auto` on accounts.failover as `manual`, keeping its provenance.

entries.consequence: Choose how much recorded history stays in the active ledger. Older records move to sealed, signed archives on this computer; this setting does not delete them. Tool activity audit separately decides which completion summaries are recorded.
capabilities: A larger active window makes more recent history available without opening an archive.
Keep everything leaves all recorded events in the active ledger.
risks: A larger active ledger takes more storage and can cost more time to verify or query. The effect depends on the amount of history and this computer.
Keep everything has no size limit, so storage use grows with recorded activity.
A smaller active window requires opening signed archives to inspect older records.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/audit-retention.js resolvePreset()/retentionPlan() decide when the live window is over its limit; src/lib/audit.js rollArchiveOnce() moves exactly one event to sealed storage per append and advances the signed boundary inside the same writer transaction that removes it. An unreadable or unknown value resolves to keeping everything, never to a larger deletion.

entries.consequence: Every message your agents send each other is checked for anything that looks like a password or key, and a message that trips the check is refused rather than stored. This decides how strict that check is. The middle setting permits known Fleet error codes and tool names that resemble secrets.
capabilities: On "Allow code names", agents fixing the vault can quote the error code they are looking at to each other instead of having the message refused.
On "Off", no message between agents is inspected or refused, which is the fastest setting and the only one that never refuses a message you meant to send.
risks: On "Off", a password or key an agent happens to include is written into durable message history exactly as typed, and nothing warns you.
On "Refuse look-alikes", ordinary messages about this product's own error codes are refused, and the agent has to reword them to say anything.
entries.enforcedBy: src/lib/agent-comms/history.js

entries.consequence: Compatibility name for agent.agent_api. Only means ToolsEnabled only, Optimized means ToolsEnabled with a few Claude native tools (Claude only), Enabled means both full tool sets, and Disabled means Native tools only. Settings shows the canonical Available tool sets row. Existing role and permission limits still apply, and existing sessions keep their captured choice until restarted.
capabilities: Choose whether new assistants use ToolsEnabled services, provider tools, or both.
risks: Sessions using Native tools only cannot call ToolsEnabled services or use roles that require its functions.

entries.consequence: Wait this many milliseconds to collect activity records into a batch. A tool still waits for its required record to be durable before it answers.
capabilities: Collect simultaneous activity into fewer writes when many assistants are working.
risks: Longer waits add delay before a queued tool call can receive its audit receipt.

entries.consequence: Limit how many activity records share one writer transaction. Larger batches reduce writer overhead when many assistants are active.
capabilities: Control how much activity can be recorded together during a burst of tool calls.
risks: Very large batches hold the ledger writer longer and can delay other queued calls.

entries.consequence: Zero reuses a presence result only while the encrypted vault is unchanged. A positive value also repeats the secure helper check after this many seconds. Every call checks the vault content digest; this does not cache permission, sign-in validity or revocation. Linux always consults its secure backend.
capabilities: Choose how often Windows repeats a presence check when the encrypted vault has not changed.
risks: Short intervals repeatedly start the Windows helper even when no vault record changed.

entries.consequence: Require a durable scoped policy decision for consequential tool calls. Calls without one are refused. This experimental policy is off by default.
capabilities: Require explicit scoped authorization before an assistant performs consequential tool calls.
risks: An assistant without a scoped policy authorization will be unable to perform consequential tool calls.
